source_terms: lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot
the great Indian rope trick of numbers
item.claim: Bijapurkar states the structural claim on which most of the book rests: "Consumer demand in the emerging economies is made up of lots and lots of people consuming a little bit each, adding up to a lot," where developed-market marketers "are used to working with an exactly opposite demand structure — a few people consuming a lot each, adding up to a lot." She draws the consequence explicitly: "neither the pricing paradigms nor the cost structures of their usual, tried and tested global business models are appropriate for India's demand structure." She names the counter-intuitive consequence the "great Indian rope trick of numbers" — a small penetration of a large population produces a large absolute market, so lower-income groups can out-consume higher-income groups in absolute terms.

mechanism.text: Business models encode assumptions about consumption per head. A retail format sized for a catchment that consumes a lot per head will not reach viability in a catchment that consumes little per head, regardless of how many people are in it — which is why, on her account, the first organised retail forays failed and why a small-format chain with an aggregated back end succeeded by "mimicking the structure of the customer demand".

scope.conditions: Stated for India and for emerging markets more generally, on data to 2008. Bijapurkar draws the general form from the BRIC comparison — economies "individually poor but collectively rich" — and cites Goldman Sachs's *Dreaming with the BRICs*.

caveats.text: the two-wheeler evidence was inspected and it holds. Figure 4.1 (rural two-wheeler market) shows penetration falling 42 / 25 / 10 / 2.7 per cent across income groups while household counts rise 7 / 18 / 63 / 66 million, giving two-wheeler numbers of 3.8 / 4.5 / 6.4 / 1.8 million. The lower-middle group therefore does have about 1.6 times the units of the high-income group, exactly as the text claims. Source: Indian Readership Survey 2008

the general claim about business models is argued from a small number of Indian cases (Subhiksha, shampoo sachets, community telephony) with no failure cases and no financial detail. Subhiksha in particular is presented as a success; the chain collapsed shortly after this edition was published, which the book could not know and which is recorded here because the case is load-bearing
SEVERE FRESHNESS RISK. Every figure supporting this object is 2008 or earlier and predates mobile data, e-commerce and digital payments in India

Adjacency to sk_rbwl_0010 recorded without a graph edge: why the fixed offer is mis-sized. The original extraction used a 'supports' relation, which SPEC-03 does not define; no permitted relation expresses it from this object's side, so it is kept as an observation rather than expressed as a fabricated edge.

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: The structural claim is supported by named large-sample survey data; the business-model consequence is argued from a handful of cases without financials.

source_stated_problems: business models encode a consumption-per-head assumption that fails silently in a market with the opposite structure
source_stated_remedies: design the business system to mimic the structure of the demand rather than adapting an offer designed for the opposite structure

positive: shampoo sachets creating a 'party pack' market as large as the bottled market rather than a trial-pack market

source_terms: India is merely a geographic expression
item.claim: Bijapurkar argues that "India" is not a usable market construct and that the analyst must build one: "the onus is on them to define what their India is, and translate the geographic idea into a well-defined construct of a consumer market." She develops this into the book's recurring device, "my target India", and supplies the variables from which one is assembled — consumer classes, urban versus rural, states, age cohorts and the five economies — arguing that population-stratum definitions (metro, small town, semi-urban, rural) are "no longer wise" because development has created oases that do not follow town size. She illustrates with three firms defining non-overlapping target Indias: Hindustan Unilever taking "least developed India" — deeply rural, media-dark, low-literacy — for its utensil and fabric care growth; ICICI Bank taking developed, well-off rural India for wealth management; and a typical Fortune 500 defaulting to the rich urban educated "like anywhere in the world consumer who happens to be in India."

mechanism.text: A market construct inherited as a given carries somebody else's segmentation and somebody else's idea of what varies. Constructing it deliberately from named variables forces the firm's own competencies into the definition, which is what makes two firms' target Indias differ legitimately rather than one of them being wrong.

caveats.text: the three firm examples are described without dates, revenue, outcome or source, and two are large firms whose stated strategies are matters of public record but are not cited here

the Hindustan Unilever figure — contacting 13.6 million women across 30,000 villages in eight states between 2005 and 2006 for the detergent business alone — is the most specific operational number in the chapter and is given without a source
the argument is a reframing rather than a method: it says what a target-market definition must be built from, not how to choose among the resulting definitions. The book does not claim otherwise

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Firm examples without sources or outcomes.

source_stated_problems: an inherited market construct imports somebody else's segmentation and hides the firm's own competencies from the definition
source_stated_remedies: assemble the target-market construct explicitly from named variables rather than accepting a geographic or population-stratum default

positive: Hindustan Unilever's 'least developed India' for utensil and fabric care
ICICI Bank's developed, well-off rural India for high-net-worth services

item.claim: Bijapurkar argues that the expectation of a zero-sum contest between tradition and modernity, with modernity winning, was wrong, and that the observed pattern is "this as well as that": the new is adopted alongside the old in hybrid forms rather than replacing it. Her worked cases: chocolate makers failed to enter the Diwali sweets exchange with advertising, special flavours and Indian motifs, and succeeded only when small players packed individually wrapped chocolate mounds in the traditional decorated clay lamps used for the festival; ready-to-eat processed food was pre-empted not by changed food habits but by a cottage "kitchen outsourcing" sector supplying idli-dosa batter in plastic packets and home-cooked tiffin, which she analyses as "the best of both worlds — made on a micro scale, as if at home ... ready to cook (all negative labour outsourced!) but home-made (the positive labour retained!)"; and the arranged marriage becoming an "engineered" marriage rather than giving way to dating.

mechanism.text: Where a practice bundles several benefits, only some of which the new offer improves, adoption proceeds by unbundling: the disliked component is outsourced and the valued component retained. The result looks like resistance to the new offer but is actually a more precise version of the demand than the offer addressed, which is why the successful entrant is usually the one that unbundles rather than the one that substitutes.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets post-1991. Bijapurkar generalises it as "the DNA of Indian society", which is a strong culturalist framing and is treated below.

caveats.text: THE UNBUNDLING MECHANISM AND THE CULTURALIST FRAMING ARE SEPARABLE AND SHOULD BE SEPARATED. The mechanism — a bundled practice is adopted by outsourcing the disliked component and retaining the valued one — is a clean and general account. The framing that this expresses an Indian 'DNA' with 'high tolerance of ambiguity', evidenced by avatars in the Hindu pantheon and by Brahmins in Bengal being permitted fish, is essentialist, is not evidenced, and does no work the mechanism does not already do

the cases are told without dates, volumes or sources. The kitchen-outsourcing claim in particular — that it 'succeeded in pre-empting the entry of ready-to-eat processed food' — is a strong causal statement with no evidence offered

Table 9.2, 'Indian and Western Values', which sets out the culturalist framing as a two-column list, appears ONLY as an image in this copy and its content does not appear in the text. It was opened and read. It is a schematic of asserted binary contrasts (patriarchy/egalitarianism, ambiguity/clarity, dharma/individually chosen roles) with no source and no data, and it should be read as the author's summary of her own position, not as a finding

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Cases without dates or figures; the culturalist generalisation is asserted.

source_stated_problems: an offer that substitutes for a bundled practice competes with all its benefits at once, including the ones the buyer values
source_stated_remedies: unbundle: outsource the disliked component of the practice and leave the valued component with the buyer

positive: chocolate mounds packed in traditional Diwali clay lamps
idli-dosa batter in plastic packets, and home-cooked tiffin delivery

item.definition_in_origin_frame: The author's characterisation of Indian household income survey data: repeat the survey with the same questions and you get the same answers, so it is reliable; it does not measure the real thing, so it is not valid. Her operational consequence is that it is usable for grading the population and for comparing growth over time, and not for levels.

item.claim: The book states its own purpose as providing a window onto the changing Indian consumer landscape for students and general readers, and as leaving readers with questions rather than answers. It does not claim to establish causal findings about advertising effectiveness.

scope.conditions: the book's own statement of purpose

caveats.text: this matters for consumption: outcome language in the book ('the brand went on to be the largest selling') is reported commercial history, not the source's measurement of advertising's contribution
